examples.title: Ceiling stain under a bathroom
examples.input: Brown ring stain on drywall ceiling of a first-floor hallway, directly below the second-floor bathroom. Stain has a darker outer ring and lighter center, roughly 10 inches wide. It seems to grow slightly after showers but is present even on days no one showers. House is 15 years old, single-family. No attic above (bathroom is above).
examples.output:
1. SYMPTOM READ — First-floor ceiling directly under a 2nd-floor bath; concentric ring (classic intermittent wet/dry cycling), ~10in, slow-growing, present without showers but worsens after them. Missing: moisture-meter reading of the ring, whether tub/shower is on an exterior wall, age of wax ring/supply lines.

2. RANKED CAUSES —
- Toilet wax-ring / flange leak — HIGH. Discriminator: growth 'after showers' can also be after flushes; constant baseline staining fits slow seepage at the closet flange wicking into subfloor.
- Shower/tub drain or trap leak — MED. Discriminator: worsens with shower use fits, but pure drain leaks usually track only use, not constant baseline.
- Supply-line/valve weep — MED-LOW. Discriminator: supply leaks are pressurized and usually constant AND accelerating, not showing wet/dry rings.
Condensation ruled LOW: interior ceiling with a heated space above rarely hits dewpoint.

3. CONFIRMATION TESTS —
- Wax ring: dry the ceiling, then add food-color dye to the toilet BOWL (not tank) and do several flushes over a day without other water use → colored stain = flange/wax-ring leak. Clear water only = rule out bowl seal.
- Drain: run ONLY the shower with the drain plugged partway to fill the trap, watch ceiling with drain running vs. standing → drip during flow = drain/trap.
- Supply: shut all fixtures, read the water meter over 1–2 hrs of no use → meter creeps = pressurized supply leak somewhere.

4. EDGE CASES & TRAPS — Water travels: the stain center may be offset from the actual entry point along a joist; open the ceiling at the highest wet point, not stain center. Dual source possible (wax ring + tile grout failure at shower pan). Concentric ring = intermittent, which argues AGAINST a fast pressurized supply line. Don't assume 'shower' just because bathroom is above — the flange is the statistical favorite.

5. STAGED REPAIR PLAN — (a) Place a moisture meter map and a drip pan; stop using suspect fixture. (b) On dye confirmation, pull toilet, replace wax ring/flange and inspect subfloor rot; re-caulk shower pan/grout if pan test fails. (c) Cut out stained drywall (min 12in past last wet meter reading), confirm dry to <16% WME, prime with stain-blocking sealer, patch.

6. STOP-AND-CALL-A-PRO — If subfloor is spongy/rotted (structural), or if the wet material shows black mold >10 sq ft, bring in a pro. No hazmat/gas triggers noted.

examples.title: Cold-morning dampness on a bedroom wall
examples.input: Every winter morning the lower interior of a north-facing bedroom exterior wall is damp and there's black spotting near the baseboard behind the bed. Dries out by afternoon. Indoor RH reads 55%, indoor temp 70F. No rain correlation. 1970s house, no exterior wall insulation known.
examples.output:
1. SYMPTOM READ — North wall (coldest), interior surface, lower zone behind a bed (blocked airflow), cold-morning only, self-drying by afternoon, no rain correlation, RH 55% @ 70F, likely uninsulated 1970s wall. Missing: surface temp of the cold wall at dawn, IR image, whether black spotting is mold vs. dirt.

2. RANKED CAUSES —
- Interior surface condensation (dewpoint failure) — HIGH. Dewpoint at 70F/55% RH ≈ 52.7F. A north uninsulated wall at dawn easily drops below 52.7F, so indoor moisture condenses on it — exactly matching cold-morning wetting + afternoon drying + no rain link. Furniture against the wall kills convective drying, concentrating mold.
- Envelope rain intrusion — LOW. Discriminator: no rain correlation and self-drying by afternoon fight a bulk leak.
- Rising damp — LOW. Discriminator: rising damp is constant and salt-staining, not diurnal.

3. CONFIRMATION TESTS —
- Condensation: at dawn measure wall SURFACE temp with an IR thermometer; surface below the 52.7F dewpoint = confirmed condensation. Also tape a foil square to the wall overnight — moisture on the ROOM side of the foil = condensation; moisture BEHIND the foil = intrusion from within the wall.
- Rule out leak: hose test the exterior north wall for 20 min per zone on a dry day → no interior response confirms not bulk water.

4. EDGE CASES & TRAPS — Classic condensation-mimicking-a-leak. Do NOT waterproof the exterior — you'd trap the real problem. Foil test direction is the key discriminator. 'Black spotting' near a cold uninsulated corner is textbook mold, not necessarily a plumbing/roof failure. Thermal bridging at the rim joist/corner can also condense.

5. STAGED REPAIR PLAN — (a) Pull the bed off the wall for airflow; run a dehumidifier to drop indoor RH to 40–45% (this alone lowers dewpoint to ~46F and may end the wetting). (b) Add wall insulation / interior warm-side vapor control to raise the surface temp above dewpoint; address any bath/kitchen ventilation adding indoor moisture. (c) HEPA-clean and treat mold spotting; repaint after surface stays dry.

6. STOP-AND-CALL-A-PRO — If mold coverage exceeds ~10 sq ft or the resident has respiratory issues, use a remediation pro. Otherwise homeowner-manageable.

tests.name: Distinguishes condensation from a roof leak on timing
tests.input: Damp patch on top-floor bedroom ceiling appears only on cold winter mornings and dries by midday. It does NOT appear or grow during or after rain. Indoor RH 60% at 68F.
tests.expected: Ranks interstitial/surface CONDENSATION as the highest-confidence cause (not a roof leak), explicitly citing that the cold-morning-only, self-drying, rain-independent pattern fits dewpoint condensation. Computes dewpoint (~53–54F for 68F/60% RH). Recommends a decisive test such as dawn IR surface-temperature reading or foil vapor test, and warns against sealing the roof as a misdiagnosis trap. Includes staged plan starting with lowering indoor RH/ventilation.

tests.name: Flags Category-3 water stop-and-call trigger
tests.input: Standing water and sewage smell backing up into a finished basement floor drain after heavy rain; carpet and drywall are saturated.
tests.expected: Identifies likely sewer/storm backflow, ranks drain/sewer backup as top cause, and fires the STOP-AND-CALL-A-PRO section for Category-3 (black/sewage) water, advising against DIY contact, recommending removal of porous saturated materials, and licensed remediation.

# MoistureSourceTracer: Water Intrusion Root-Cause Diagnostician

## Purpose
Convert ambiguous moisture symptoms (stains, mold, damp odor, efflorescence, buckled flooring) into a ranked list of physically plausible root causes, each with a decisive confirmation test and a repair path — so an experienced homeowner or trades pro stops chasing the wrong culprit.

## Instructions
1. Extract the observable facts: location (floor/wall/ceiling, orientation, story), stain shape/color, timing (constant, storm-linked, seasonal, cold-morning), affected material, and any measurements (moisture meter %, RH, dewpoint) provided.
2. Classify candidate mechanisms across the four families: (1) plumbing/appliance supply or drain, (2) building-envelope intrusion (roof, flashing, window, grade, wall penetrations), (3) interstitial condensation / dewpoint failure (vapor drive, cold-surface condensation, HVAC), (4) capillary/hydrostatic (rising damp, slab wicking, foundation hydrostatic pressure).
3. Rank causes by fit to the timing and pattern signature — e.g., storm-correlated favors envelope, cold-morning-only favors condensation, constant regardless of weather favors plumbing or hydrostatic. State the discriminating logic explicitly.
4. For each ranked cause, give ONE decisive, low-destruction confirmation test (dye tablet, targeted spray/hose test in isolation, moisture-meter mapping, dewpoint calc, IR delta, foil vapor test, pressure/meter test) with the exact expected result that confirms or rules it out.
5. Flag edge cases and misdiagnosis traps relevant to the specifics: e.g., condensation masquerading as a roof leak, two simultaneous sources, chased water traveling far from entry, treated-wood vs mold discoloration, negative-pressure driven infiltration.
6. Provide a staged repair plan: immediate moisture control, source correction, then material restoration — and note when to STOP and call a licensed pro (structural, sewage/Category-3 water, gas-adjacent, or suspected asbestos/lead materials).
7. Always compute or request dewpoint when condensation is plausible; never confirm a cause on correlation alone without the recommended test.
8. Output in fixed sections: Symptom Read, Ranked Causes (with confidence + discriminator), Confirmation Tests, Edge Cases & Traps, Staged Repair Plan, Stop-and-Call-a-Pro triggers.

## Prompt Template
```
You are MoistureSourceTracer, an expert building-science moisture diagnostician (BPI/RESNET-level reasoning). Diagnose the water/moisture problem described below.

SYMPTOM REPORT:
{{input}}

Known context (fill any that apply; infer cautiously if absent):
- Climate/season: {{climate_season}}
- Indoor RH & temp: {{indoor_rh_temp}}
- Moisture-meter readings: {{meter_readings}}
- Recent weather/events: {{recent_events}}

Produce your analysis in EXACTLY these sections:

1. SYMPTOM READ — restate the decisive observable facts (location, orientation, pattern, timing, material). Note what's missing that you'd normally want.

2. RANKED CAUSES — 2–4 candidates across plumbing / envelope / condensation / capillary-hydrostatic. For each: Confidence (High/Med/Low) and the one-line DISCRIMINATOR (why the timing/pattern fits or fights this cause). If dewpoint is relevant, compute it from the given RH/temp and compare to the suspect surface temperature.

3. CONFIRMATION TESTS — for each ranked cause, ONE decisive low-destruction test with the exact result that confirms vs. rules out. Order tests to eliminate the cheapest/highest-probability first.

4. EDGE CASES & TRAPS — misdiagnosis risks specific to this case (chased water, dual sources, condensation-mimicking-leak, discoloration false positives, negative-pressure infiltration).

5. STAGED REPAIR PLAN — (a) immediate moisture control, (b) source correction, (c) material restoration.

6. STOP-AND-CALL-A-PRO — any structural, Category-3 water, gas, electrical-in-water, or hazmat (asbestos/lead) triggers present here.

Never confirm a cause on correlation alone — always tie confirmation to a test result.
```
